verdict.headline: Two inflation reports arrive with September's oil and shipping costs outside both of them
verdict.label: Brent traded above $102 in a fifth straight gain and supertanker rates reached a record near $800,000 a day, while the ten-year held above 4.818% near 4.84% and equity futures sat close to flat into the August PPI print
verdict.rationale_short:
August PPI lands at 8:30 a.m. and August CPI follows Friday, and neither can contain the input that has moved this market all week. Brent for November delivery traded above $102 in a fifth straight session of gains and WTI above $97, while the cost of moving a barrel rose faster than the barrel itself: the benchmark supertanker rate from the Middle East to China reached a record near $800,000 a day after Iran struck ten ships near Hormuz and the US sank five Iranian tankers, the largest shipping attacks of the six-month conflict. Both prints cover August, before any of that.

The consensus into the release is for headline producer inflation at 5.3% year over year against 4.7% in July, with core at 4.6% against 4.2% — an acceleration is already expected, which sets the bar the reaction has to clear. That makes the print asymmetric in a way the number alone does not show. A hot August figure says pass-through was running before September's energy cost arrived. A cool one says less than it appears, because the input that would drive it is not in the data yet and the September print that can carry $100 crude is not released until October, after the September 16 decision.

The rates picture supports the read but does not settle it. The ten-year broke 4.818% on Wednesday to reach 4.857%, its highest in three years, and has not given the level back, sitting near 4.84% with yields steady into the data. A level surviving one quiet morning is a low bar. Against the inflation-scare framing, the dollar slipped to a four-month low rather than being bid, gold traded above $4,400, and the oil rally paused into the print rather than extending — none of which is what a market convinced of an imminent policy response looks like. Equity futures are close to flat, with Nasdaq-100 contracts down 0.3% the only index pointing lower.

The policy backdrop moved with it. Market pricing for a quarter-point hike on September 16 has risen from roughly 56% to about 61%, and New York Fed President John Williams signaled openness to a hike at the September 15-16 meeting, a shift from favoring a hold. The committee is in blackout through September 17, so neither print gets framed by an official before the decision. A separate fiscal input arrived overnight: a pledged $5,000 dividend to every adult American contingent on Republicans holding both chambers in November, pointed at tariff revenue of about $154.5 billion in the first ten months of fiscal 2026 — even a hundred million recipients would cost $500 billion against that. It is contingent on a November 3 election the House is not currently projected to deliver, so it is a tail input rather than a base case, but it lands on a long end that has spent the week repricing exactly that question.

What would change the picture: the split of the reaction across the curve rather than the headline. A hot number that lifts the two-year and leaves the ten-year near 4.84% is the Fed being trusted to respond. A hot number that carries the ten-year toward 5.00% while the front end stays put is inflation the market does not expect the Fed to fully offset. A close back under 4.818% on the ten-year would say Wednesday's break was one day's news rather than a repricing. On the thirty-year, 5.33% — August 18's nineteen-year high — is the level above 5.30%.
verdict.lede_short: August PPI lands at 8:30 a.m. and CPI follows Friday, but neither can contain what has actually moved this market: Brent above $102 in a fifth straight gain, and a record supertanker rate near $800,000 a day after attacks near Hormuz. The ten-year has held its break above 4.818% at about 4.84% with futures near flat. Watch where the reaction sits on the curve — a hot print that lifts the two-year is different information from one that carries the ten-year toward 5.00%.

watchlist_mentions.note: Reports fiscal first-quarter results after the close on consensus of about $19.13 billion in revenue, against the $638 billion remaining performance obligation reported last quarter, with options implying roughly a 10% move. The question is conversion — how fast backlog becomes revenue and what the capex to serve it costs. It is the largest single-name read on AI infrastructure spending this week and it lands with Nasdaq-100 futures the only major contract pointing lower.

Named Nebius its preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner on September 8, integrating Nebius compute and inference inside the Palantir perimeter for commercial customers, with no financial terms disclosed. Palantir fell 0.45% and Nebius 1.45% on the announcement — a sovereign-compute arrangement that moved neither stock, which is a reading on how much of the AI infrastructure buildout is already in the price.

WTI for October traded above $97 with Brent for November above $102, a fifth straight session of gains, though the rally paused into the inflation data rather than extending. The tracked level remains $100 on WTI. Supertanker rates on the Gulf-to-China route at a record near $800,000 a day are the separate cost channel to watch alongside the barrel.

Gold traded above $4,400 at about $4,405.88 into the inflation prints, up 0.18%, while the dollar slipped to a four-month low. A bid in gold alongside a soft dollar is consistent with an inflation and fiscal concern rather than with a policy-response repricing, which would more usually lift the dollar.

Held near $78,300, little changed from Wednesday and still below $80,000 for a ninth session. It has not taken a bid from the long-end selloff or from the record in gold, which continues to leave it detached from both the haven trade and the rates trade.

trade_setups.asset: The shape of the curve's reaction to August PPI
trade_setups.thesis: Consensus is for headline producer inflation at 5.3% year over year against 4.7% in July and core at 4.6% against 4.2%, so an acceleration is already expected and the number alone carries less information than where the reaction sits. A hot print that lifts the two-year and leaves the ten-year near 4.84% is the market trusting the Fed to respond; a hot print that carries the ten-year higher while the front end stays put is inflation the market does not expect the Fed to fully offset. The evidence is not one-sided: the dollar at a four-month low and gold above $4,400 argue against a clean policy-response repricing.
trade_setups.entry: 4.818% is the level that broke Wednesday and has held; 5.00% is the next round threshold above it. The two-year at 4.42% is the comparison that separates the two readings.
trade_setups.invalidation: A close back under 4.818% on the ten-year would say Wednesday's break was one day's news rather than a repricing.
trade_setups.horizon: The first hour of trade, then Friday's CPI into the September 16 decision

trade_setups.asset: Freight cost as a channel separate from the crude price
trade_setups.thesis: Supertanker earnings on the Middle East-to-China route reached a record near $800,000 a day after the largest shipping attacks of the six-month conflict. Freight raises the delivered cost of every cargo rather than only the marginal barrel, and it responds to shipping risk rather than to production, so it can keep tightening even if crude stalls. Hormuz transits had recovered toward 7 million barrels a day by late August, which argues the constraint is currently risk premium and shipping capacity rather than an outright supply shortage.
trade_setups.entry: The record near $800,000 a day is the reference; Brent holding above $100 is the second variable. October data is the first release that can carry either.
trade_setups.invalidation: Rates easing while Brent holds above $100 would say the premium is narrowing to the crude price itself rather than broadening into a general shipping cost.
trade_setups.horizon: Into October data, which the September 16 meeting will not see

trade_setups.asset: Oracle's backlog conversion after the close
trade_setups.thesis: Consensus is about $19.13 billion in revenue against the $638 billion remaining performance obligation reported last quarter, with options implying roughly a 10% move. The reported backlog is not the question; the rate at which it converts to revenue and the capital expenditure required to serve it are. The result lands with Nasdaq-100 futures down 0.3% and the other major contracts near flat, so it is the clearest read this week on whether AI infrastructure spending is being valued on bookings or on delivery.
trade_setups.entry: Cloud infrastructure growth against management's 58% to 65% guidance range is the line the print is measured against; capex commentary is the second variable.
trade_setups.invalidation: Growth inside the guided range with unchanged capex would say the backlog question is a timing matter rather than a funding one.
trade_setups.horizon: After Thursday's close, into Friday's session
